title: Results
text: This section presents qualitative results from the deployed Off-the-Beaten-Path Travel Recommender, comparing BM25 and ModernBERT (FAISS) retrieval on real queries against the live system.

BM25 Query 1 Map


Interpretation: The top two results (Alps, Pieralongia) are correctly grounded in the Dolomites, showing BM25’s strength on explicit queries. Beyond that, relevance degrades quickly—results 3–10 span the Caribbean, North America, Scandinavia, East Asia, and Oceania, retrieved mainly for hiking/camping/mountain keyword density rather than alignment with Italy specifically. This illustrates BM25’s key limitation: it scores query terms independently and doesn’t enforce joint constraints across activity, terrain, and location.
LLM explanations for the top results confirm this: Alps and Pieralongia both cite specific Dolomites trails and landmarks (Seceda, Alpe di Siusi, via ferrata routes), while the U.S. Virgin Islands explanation reveals the activity match without the geographic one—hiking/camping/climbing content, wrong hemisphere.

ModernBERT Query 1 Map


Interpretation: The top two results match exactly on both geography and activity. As rank increases, results broaden gradually by concept rather than degrading abruptly—Rome/Abruzzo stays relevant via dolomite-peak and national-park language even though it’s the wrong region, and lower ranks drift toward general Italy travel content and lighter, non-alpine hiking (Amalfi Coast, Cinque Terre, Florence). This smooth relaxation of specificity contrasts with BM25’s sharper, noisier drop-off.
Key takeaway: ModernBERT preserves mountain-hiking intent even as geography drifts and avoids the activity-only false positives (e.g., tropical islands) that BM25 produces, making it better suited to queries where intent matters more than exact wording.

Interpretation: BM25 reliably surfaces coastal destinations but ranks broad regions and cities (Maine, Boston, San Francisco) above smaller towns despite the “small” constraint, and repeats the same region multiple times due to keyword density rather than destination granularity—showing it emphasizes keyword frequency over interpretive intent like “slow travel.”
LLM explanations show Maine’s result draws on Ogunquit/Kennebunkport/Wells content (seafood, museums, seaside activities), Boston’s draws on nearby Rockport rather than the city itself, and Grayton Beach is one of the strongest true town-level matches in the set.

Interpretation: The top result, South Shore (MA), reflects the full query intent—quiet towns, museums, sailing, a relaxed pace—and Maine/Northern Michigan follow for similar reasons. Notably, France (La Rochelle / Île de Ré) ranks highly despite being geographically distant, showing the model generalizing “slow seaside living” across countries rather than matching on location keywords. Lower ranks broaden toward city- and country-level entries (Sydney, Charleston, California, Italy) that partially relax the “small town” constraint.
Key takeaway: ModernBERT captures experiential and lifestyle intent (slow travel, local culture, town scale) that BM25’s keyword matching misses, and relaxes constraints gradually rather than dropping into unrelated results—making it the stronger choice for exploratory, feel-based travel queries.

title: Off-the-Beaten-Path Travel Recommender
text:
Application Link
ML Travel Recommendation Website






Warning



Live webpage is no longer deployed. See results for video and written examples.





Introduction
Popular travel platforms often optimize for popularity, reinforcing the same well-known destinations and experiences. This project takes a different approach.
The Off-the-Beaten-Path Travel Recommender is a semantic search and retrieval system designed to surface less-crowded, locally authentic, and contextually relevant travel destinations by learning directly from long-form travel blog content. Instead of relying on predefined destination rankings or user reviews, the system analyzes narrative travel writing to identify places that align with exploratory, low-tourism intent.
The project combines traditional information retrieval with modern transformer-based semantic search, exposed through a lightweight API for interactive exploration.



What This System Does

Searches thousands of travel blog posts describing destinations around the world
Supports both keyword-based and semantic search modes
Captures nuanced intent such as quiet, local, hidden, or underrated
Returns destination-level results with geographic metadata and source context
Generates natural-language explanations for why results match a query

The system is designed to be modular, interpretable, and extensible—making it suitable for research, experimentation, or deployment as a discovery-focused travel tool.



Core Components

Lexical Retrieval (BM25)
A fast, keyword-based baseline search using BM25 scoring. This mode prioritizes direct term overlap and serves as a strong reference point for traditional search behavior.


Semantic Retrieval (ModernBERT + FAISS)
A transformer-based semantic search pipeline using ModernBERT embeddings indexed with FAISS. This enables retrieval based on meaning rather than exact wording, allowing the system to understand experiential intent and contextual relevance across diverse travel narratives.


API Layer
A FastAPI backend exposes a unified /search endpoint, allowing clients to switch between retrieval models with a simple configuration flag. The API returns structured results, excerpts, and optional LLM-generated explanations.


Data & Hosting
Blog metadata lives in an AWS RDS PostgreSQL database, and precomputed ModernBERT embeddings are stored in an AWS S3 bucket and loaded into a FAISS index at API startup. The Streamlit frontend and FastAPI backend are each deployed as their own Hugging Face Space.




Use Cases

Discovering lesser-known destinations aligned with personal travel style
Comparing lexical vs semantic retrieval behavior
Experimenting with modern NLP techniques in a real-world domain
Serving as a foundation for future recommendation or personalization systems

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text: This project constructs its retrieval corpus from long-form travel blog content, with an emphasis on destination-centric narratives rather than short reviews or structured listings. The pipeline performs collection, cleaning, feature extraction, and geospatial enrichment before persisting records into a cloud-hosted relational database for downstream retrieval and modeling.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Data Sources
The primary data source is public WordPress-hosted travel blogs, discovered via SerpAPI-powered Google searches (e.g. travel site:wordpress.com). This surfaces organically authored, destination-focused travel writing rather than curated travel platforms.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Blog Discovery & Page Enumeration
Each result returned by SerpAPI is treated as a candidate blog domain. For each domain, the pipeline looks for a WordPress sitemap at common paths (/post-sitemap.xml, /sitemap.xml, /sitemap-1.xml, /sitemap_index.xml). If found, all listed URLs are extracted and filtered to drop pagination, category/tag/author pages, feeds, admin paths, and non-HTML media—leaving only individual post URLs. This sitemap-first strategy enables efficient, respectful crawling without brute-force URL guessing.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Content Scraping
Each candidate post is fetched with requests and parsed with BeautifulSoup to extract:

Page title, meta description, and author (when available)
Main body text (paragraph-level content)

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Text Cleaning & Normalization
Raw content is normalized before storage: Unicode and quote/dash standardization, punctuation and symbol removal, lowercasing, whitespace collapsing, and replacement of symbols (e.g., & → and). This produces a clean text field used for both BM25 indexing and embedding generation.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Feature Engineering

Named Entity Recognition (NER)
spaCy NER is applied to each post’s title and description to extract a plausible geopolitical or location entity (GPE, LOC), preferring multi-word place names and combining consecutive location entities where possible. This produces a structured location_name field.


Geocoding
Extracted location names are geocoded to latitude/longitude via ArcGIS (through geopy), with a short delay between requests. Locations that fail to resolve are logged and skipped rather than blocking ingestion.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
URL & Content Filtering
Pagination, feeds, tag/category pages, and non-HTML resources are excluded up front. Records with no resolvable location are not persisted, and duplicate page_url values are rejected at the database level.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Database Persistence
Cleaned and enriched records are written to an AWS RDS PostgreSQL database via SQLAlchemy. Each record includes:

Blog domain and page URL
Page title, description, and author
Extracted destination name
Latitude and longitude
Fully cleaned textual content

The schema enforces uniqueness on page_url, and duplicate inserts are caught and skipped.

title: Data Collection & Cleaning
text:
Embeddings for Semantic Search
ModernBERT embeddings for the cleaned corpus are computed offline and uploaded to an AWS S3 bucket, separate from the RDS metadata store. The API loads these embeddings from S3 at startup to build the FAISS index used for semantic search (see Methods).

title: Methods
text: This project implements a dual-retrieval search system for travel discovery, combining a traditional lexical baseline with a modern semantic embedding pipeline. Both retrieval methods operate over the same cleaned and enriched travel blog corpus and are exposed through a unified FastAPI service, deployed as a Hugging Face Space.

title: Methods
text:
Lexical Retrieval: BM25

Index Construction
At API startup, all blog records are loaded from the AWS RDS PostgreSQL database and cached in memory. For each post, the title, description, and full cleaned content are concatenated into a single searchable document, tokenized with a lightweight regex tokenizer (lowercased, alphanumeric tokens only), and indexed with rank-bm25.


Query Processing & Scoring
A query is tokenized the same way as the corpus, scored against every document, and ranked by descending BM25 score. The top-k results are returned, each with destination name, country, coordinates, BM25 score, source metadata (title, author, URLs), and a short content preview. Scores are returned directly to the client to preserve interpretability.

title: Methods
text:
Semantic Retrieval: ModernBERT + FAISS

Embeddings
Document embeddings are computed offline using a ModernBERT-based encoder and stored in an AWS S3 bucket, decoupled from the RDS metadata store. Embeddings are mean-pooled and L2-normalized so that L2 distance approximates cosine similarity.


FAISS Index Construction
At API startup, blog metadata is loaded from RDS and the precomputed embeddings are loaded from S3. A FAISS IndexFlatL2 index is built over the embeddings, decoupling embedding generation from request-time serving for low-latency search.


Query Processing & Retrieval
The query is embedded with the same model and searched against the FAISS index. Results are ranked by ascending L2 distance (lower = more similar) and returned with destination name, country, coordinates, distance score, source metadata, and content preview.

title: Methods
text:
Result Explanation with LLMs
To improve transparency, the system can optionally generate a short natural-language explanation for each of the top 3 results. A prompt containing the user query and the retrieved post’s full text is sent to DeepSeek-V3 via the Hugging Face Inference API, which returns a concise explanation referencing the destination. If the call fails, the API returns a placeholder (“Explanation unavailable.”) rather than failing the whole request.

title: Methods
text:
Unified API Design
Both BM25 and FAISS retrieval are exposed through a single /search endpoint; the retrieval strategy and explanation toggle are set via fields in the request payload. This allows direct comparison between lexical and semantic retrieval and leaves room for future hybrid or re-ranking approaches.

title: Methods
text:
Summary

BM25: fast, interpretable keyword-based search over an RDS-backed corpus
ModernBERT + FAISS: context-aware semantic retrieval over S3-backed embeddings
LLM explanations: human-readable interpretability via DeepSeek-V3

Together, these components form a flexible, extensible search system for exploratory, off-the-beaten-path travel discovery.
